summary.text: Construct Pell-type pairs \((p_n,q_n)\) satisfying \(p_n^2+2p_nq_n-q_n^2=1\); then \(p_n/q_n\) approximates \(\sqrt2-1\) from above within \(1/q_n^2\), so for every \(1\le k\le q_n\) the relevant floor equals \((kp_n-1)/q_n\). Grouping this rational sum by quotient values and using the oddness of \(p_n\) yields the recurrence \(S(p_{n+1},q_{n+1})=2+S(p_n,q_n)\), hence the selected partial sums equal \(2(n+1)\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
\alpha=\sqrt2-1,
\qquad
a(N)=\sum_{k=1}^N(-1)^{\lfloor k\alpha\rfloor}.
\]
Since \(\sqrt2>1\), we have \(\alpha>0\), so for every \(k\geq 1\) the integer \(\lfloor k\alpha\rfloor\) is nonnegative. Thus the displayed powers of \(-1\) have their usual meaning with nonnegative integer exponents.

We shall construct infinitely many indices \(N\) at which \(a(N)\) can be evaluated exactly and tends to infinity.

### 1. A rational auxiliary sum

For positive integers \(p,q\), define
\[
R(p,q)=\sum_{k=1}^{q}(-1)^{\left\lfloor\frac{kp-1}{q}\right\rfloor}.
\]
Here the floor is redundant because \((kp-1)/q\) is interpreted as integer division; equivalently, the exponent is the quotient in Euclidean division of \(kp-1\) by \(q\).

We first rewrite this sum by counting how often each exponent occurs. For \(1\leq k\leq q\), put
\[
e(k)=\left\lfloor\frac{kp-1}{q}\right\rfloor.
\]
Because \(kp-1<pq\), one has \(0\leq e(k)<p\). For an integer \(j\) with \(0\leq j<p\), the equality \(e(k)=j\) is equivalent to
\[
jq\leq kp-1<(j+1)q.
\]
Since all quantities here are integers, this is equivalent to
\[
jq<kp\leq (j+1)q.
\]
Dividing by the positive integer \(p\), the integers \(k\) satisfying this condition are precisely those in the interval
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{jq}{p}\right\rfloor<k\leq
\left\lfloor\frac{(j+1)q}{p}\right\rfloor.
\]
Consequently, the number of such \(k\) is
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{(j+1)q}{p}\right\rfloor-
\left\lfloor\frac{jq}{p}\right\rfloor.
\]
Grouping the terms of \(R(p,q)\) according to the value of \(e(k)\), we obtain
\[
R(p,q)=C(p,q),                                      \tag{1}
\]
where
\[
C(p,q)=\sum_{j=0}^{p-1}(-1)^j
\left(
\left\lfloor\frac{(j+1)q}{p}\right\rfloor-
\left\lfloor\frac{jq}{p}\right\rfloor
\right).
\]

We need two elementary reduction identities.

First, if \(p,r>0\), then
\[
C(p,2p+r)=2\sum_{j=0}^{p-1}(-1)^j+C(p,r).           \tag{2}
\]
Indeed, for every \(j\geq0\),
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{j(2p+r)}p\right\rfloor
=2j+\left\lfloor\frac{jr}{p}\right\rfloor.
\]
Taking the difference of this formula at \(j+1\) and at \(j\) contributes \(2\), in addition to the corresponding difference for \(r\). Summing with coefficient \((-1)^j\) gives (2).

Second, if \(s,r>0\), then
\[
R(2r+s,r)=R(s,r).                                   \tag{3}
\]
For \(1\leq k\leq r\),
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{k(2r+s)-1}{r}\right\rfloor
=2k+\left\lfloor\frac{ks-1}{r}\right\rfloor.
\]
The two exponents on the two sides differ by the even integer \(2k\), so their powers of \(-1\) agree. Summing over \(k\) proves (3).

Now suppose that positive integers \(s,r,p,q\) satisfy
\[
p=2r+s,\qquad q=2p+r,
\]
and suppose also that \(p\) is odd. Since the alternating sum of an odd number of terms beginning with \(1\) is \(1\),
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{p-1}(-1)^j=1.
\]
Using (1), (2), and (3), we therefore get the important recurrence
\[
\begin{aligned}
R(p,q)
 &=C(p,2p+r)\\
 &=2+C(p,r)\\
 &=2+R(p,r)\\
 &=2+R(2r+s,r)\\
 &=2+R(s,r).
\end{aligned}                                       \tag{4}
\]

### 2. Pell-type pairs and exact evaluation of the rational sums

Define sequences of positive integers \((p_n,q_n)\) recursively by
\[
(p_0,q_0)=(1,2),
\]
and, for \(n\geq0\),
\[
p_{n+1}=2q_n+p_n,
\qquad
q_{n+1}=2p_{n+1}+q_n.                               \tag{5}
\]
Both sequences are positive. Moreover, every \(p_n\) is odd: \(p_0=1\) is odd, and \(p_{n+1}=2q_n+p_n\) has the same parity as \(p_n\).

Apply (4) with
\[
s=p_n,\quad r=q_n,\quad p=p_{n+1},\quad q=q_{n+1}.
\]
The defining equations (5) give exactly the hypotheses of (4), and \(p_{n+1}\) is odd. Hence
\[
R(p_{n+1},q_{n+1})=2+R(p_n,q_n).                    \tag{6}
\]
At the initial pair,
\[
R(1,2)
=(-1)^{\lfloor(1-1)/2\rfloor}
 +(-1)^{\lfloor(2-1)/2\rfloor}
=1+1=2.
\]
Induction in (6) now gives
\[
R(p_n,q_n)=2(n+1)                                   \tag{7}
\]
for every \(n\geq0\).

### 3. The Pell invariant and approximation to \(\sqrt2-1\)

The pairs in (5) satisfy
\[
p_n^2+2p_nq_n-q_n^2=1                              \tag{8}
\]
for every \(n\). For \(n=0\), this is
\[
1^2+2\cdot1\cdot2-2^2=1.
\]
For the induction step, write \(p=p_n\), \(q=q_n\),
\[
P=p_{n+1}=p+2q,
\qquad
Q=q_{n+1}=2P+q=2p+5q.
\]
A direct expansion gives
\[
P^2+2PQ-Q^2=p^2+2pq-q^2.
\]
Thus the value of this quadratic form is preserved, proving (8).

Fix \(n\), and abbreviate \(p=p_n\), \(q=q_n\), and \(x=p/q\). Dividing (8) by \(q^2\) yields
\[
x^2+2x-1=\frac1{q^2}.                              \tag{9}
\]
The number \(\alpha=\sqrt2-1\) is the positive root of
\[
t^2+2t-1=0.
\]
Accordingly,
\[
x^2+2x-1
=(x-\alpha)(x+\sqrt2+1).
\]
Combining this factorization with (9),
\[
x-\alpha=
\frac{1/q^2}{x+\sqrt2+1}.                          \tag{10}
\]
The denominator in (10) is positive, and indeed is greater than \(1\), because \(x\geq0\) and \(\sqrt2>0\). It follows that
\[
0<\frac pq-\alpha<\frac1{q^2}.                    \tag{11}
\]
Thus each \(p_n/q_n\) is a rational approximation to \(\alpha\) from above, with an error smaller than \(1/q_n^2\).

### 4. Agreement of the irrational and rational exponents

We claim that for every \(n\) and every integer \(k\) with \(1\leq k\leq q_n\),
\[
\left\lfloor k\alpha\right\rfloor
=
\left\lfloor\frac{kp_n-1}{q_n}\right\rfloor.       \tag{12}
\]
Fix \(n\), again write \(p=p_n\), \(q=q_n\), and define
\[
e=\left\lfloor\frac{kp-1}{q}\right\rfloor.
\]
By the defining inequalities for integer division,
\[
eq\leq kp-1<(e+1)q.                              \tag{13}
\]
The left inequality in (13) gives
\[
e\leq \frac{kp-1}{q}= rac{kp}{q}-\frac1q.        \tag{14}
\]
On the other hand, since \(k\leq q\), the approximation estimate (11) implies
\[
0<k\left(\frac pq-\alpha\right)<\frac{k}{q^2}
\leq\frac1q.                                        \tag{15}
\]
Therefore
\[
k\alpha
=\frac{kp}{q}-k\left(\frac pq-\alpha\right)
>\frac{kp}{q}-\frac1q
\geq e,                                              \tag{16}
\]
where the last inequality is (14).

For the upper bound, the right inequality of (13), because its terms are integers, implies
\[
kp\leq(e+1)q.
\]
Hence \(kp/q\leq e+1\). Also (11) says \(\alpha<p/q\), and \(k>0\), so
\[
k\alpha<\frac{kp}{q}\leq e+1.                    \tag{17}
\]
Together, (16) and (17) say
\[
e<k\alpha<e+1.
\]
In particular, \(e\leq k\alpha<e+1\), and therefore \(\lfloor k\alpha\rfloor=e\), proving (12). The stronger strict lower inequality is a consequence of the deliberately inserted \(-1\) in the numerator defining \(R\).

Taking \(q=q_n\), equality (12) holds for every summand with \(1\leq k\leq q_n\). Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(q_n)
&=\sum_{k=1}^{q_n}(-1)^{\lfloor k\alpha\rfloor}\\
&=\sum_{k=1}^{q_n}(-1)^{\left\lfloor(kp_n-1)/q_n\right\rfloor}\\
&=R(p_n,q_n).
\end{aligned}
\]
Using (7), we have obtained the exact values
\[
a(q_n)=2(n+1)                                      \tag{18}
\]
for every \(n\geq0\).

### 5. Unboundedness

The right-hand side of (18) tends to infinity. Explicitly, given any integer \(M\), choose a nonnegative integer \(n\) with \(n\geq\max(M,0)\). Then
\[
a(q_n)=2(n+1)>n\geq M.
\]
Thus for every integer \(M\) there exists the natural-number index \(N=q_n\) such that \(a(N)>M\). Therefore the sequence of partial sums
\[
\sum_{k=1}^N(-1)^{\lfloor k(\sqrt2-1)\rfloor}
\]
is unbounded above.
